I've had tremendous numbers of bumblebees on these and other flowers this year...must be several hives nearby because there is more than one kind. I've completely lost any fear of them. I've got some hyssop near a path which I constantly brush by and disturb them without any aggressiveness from them at all.

I found that the purple mums...if planted early and watered until the ground freezes.... can get established. My old garden had one that was over 10 years old but some years would look quite small. They are easier to plant as annuals.

For now, I'm going on the assumption that bacteria/cellular organisms/plants/etc. are a given, and we really want to be talking about intelligent life here. To me there are a few main things to consider in the idea of someday finding/being found by intelligent life:

  • What does intelligent life even look like? Our definition of life is based on our planet and solar system and galaxy. There could be all kinds of crazy shit in the universe. Life may look vastly different than anything we could possibly imagine. How will we know it when we see it? We can hardly agree on a definition of "intelligence" in the terms of a human being, so how will we know if the life we find is intelligent? We ourselves may or may not be actually intelligent in the grand scheme of what is possible for life, so the chances that intelligent life looks like us, or what we think it will be, or something we could even recognize, are slim to none.

  • How the hell are we even going to find it? The universe is HUGE. I mean FUCKING HUGE. We have no idea how common it is for life to evolve into intelligence as we know it, considering the tiny amount of the universe that we can currently explore. So the chances of contact could be very high with the right technology because intelligent life is abundant. Conversely, it could be very low even with advanced technology because intelligent life is so rare. How are we to know?

  • What are the chances that we happen to bump into it at this particular moment in this particular corner of the universe? The universe is 13.8 billion years old. As previously mentioned, we don't know how common intelligent life is. We may have missed other intelligent species by a few thousand or million or billion years in either direction. And assuming there were many in the past, if we ever make it out to where they were, how would we know their fossils and ruins when we see them?

Tldr; this is a brain-melting question with limitless aspects to consider and limitless answers.
